prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B008 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. Round 1 showed that the substance is not in dispute. Six of eight members put the lattice clock first and the other two rank it first among their alternatives, and every reservation raised is about framing, precedent and timing, not about the science. The invention is specific: a magic-wavelength optical lattice that removes Doppler and recoil shifts, lets many atoms be interrogated in parallel, and took optical clocks from the 1e-15 regime to below 1e-18. The performance has been reproduced in Sr, Yb and Hg in several national laboratories and is compared routinely. The chair asks whether this is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. It is, and the citation can say so by naming the lattice. The 2005 prize rewarded comb-based optical frequency measurement, the ability to count optical cycles. The 2012 prize rewarded control and measurement of individual quantum systems, with a single trapped ion as the working object. The lattice clock answers a different question: how to hold a large ensemble of neutral atoms with no motional shift and no net lattice perturbation, so that statistical power and accuracy improve together. Wording that centres on the lattice and the many-atom neutral-atom clock keeps that distinction explicit and says nothing about the SI second, which the Academy need not mention.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. First, the credit is a judgement: the magic-wavelength idea and the first demonstrations (Katori) are not the whole story, and NIST, PTB, SYRTE, Tokyo and others contributed to lattice clocks, ion clocks and ultrastable lasers. A two-name prize necessarily leaves some of these outside. Second, Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work sits close to the 2005 prize, so the citation must not drift towards comb metrology or clocks in general. Third, the SI redefinition is still pending, and a committee that wanted the societal payoff to be visible first could reasonably wait. I do not find this decisive, because the prize criterion concerns the invention, and the performance is already demonstrated. I also have to acknowledge that I know this technical area closely and am therefore likely to find the science easy to accept.

responses.point: Lindroth judges the lattice clock a distinct invention rather than an extension of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, while noting that this is the point on which the case is most contestable, and asks whether other lattice-clock contributors are underweighted by a two-name credit.
responses.response: I agree with your distinctness judgement and want to give the physical reason, because the committee should be able to state it plainly. The comb prize gave a ruler for optical frequency. The ion prize gave control of one quantum system. Neither addresses how to interrogate many neutral atoms with the motional and lattice shifts cancelled, which is exactly what the magic wavelength does. On the underweighted contributors I am less relaxed than my round-1 text. NIST, PTB, SYRTE and Tokyo made real contributions, but the question for the prize is who identified and demonstrated the lattice principle and who made it the accuracy leader. Katori and Ye answer those two questions. I would not add a third name to cover the wider ecosystem, since that would be a name chosen for institutional balance and not for the invention.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks trapped-ion quantum logic first, as an original proposal followed by experiment, but concedes that the experimental half (Blatt versus Wineland's group or Monroe) is a judgement and that B008 is the more compact and less disputed prize if the prior recognition is judged too uncertain.
responses.response: I share your concern about the 2012 overlap, and I think it is the real obstacle for B022: the first ion gates came from the NIST group, which the Academy has already honoured, and I cannot see an evidence-based way to credit Blatt alone for the experimental half. That leaves the Cirac and Zoller proposal as the clearest original contribution, with the experimental credit unresolved. I keep B022 as my first alternative because the proposal is sharp and I accept your point that the criterion concerns the invention, not whether a scalable computer exists. But I do not think the evidence you or I can point to resolves the Blatt allocation, so I cannot place it above the clock, where the two-name credit follows from the record.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for its prediction-to-experiment story, but accepts that the pairing mechanism is still debated, that Cao and parallel experiments sit outside the three names, and that the lattice clock is the safer and more mature choice if the committee holds to waiting.
responses.response: I read your statement as conceding the maturity point, and I think it is the right one. A prize on magic-angle graphene would honour a platform whose central question, the origin of the superconductivity, is open, and your own list of omitted names suggests the credit is not yet stable. I do not hold that the committee must always wait for a mechanism, and I accept that you can argue the discovery of the phases is already decisive. But between a candidate whose attribution and interpretation are still moving and one that has been reproduced for over a decade with a clear two-person credit, I would not move the graphene candidate above the clock. If your position shifts after round 2, I would be interested in what specific evidence on Cao or on the mechanism would do it.

responses.point: Johansson moved B008 to first after round 1, and argues that the Katori and Ye pairing captures the decisive credit but is a judgement and not a fact, with the SI second timing cutting in either direction.
responses.response: We agree on the pairing and on the status of the credit. On timing, I would go slightly beyond your position: the redefinition is not a reason to wait, but neither should it feature in the citation. If the Academy cites the redefinition and the vote slips or is reformulated, the prize text ages badly, whereas a citation about the lattice invention stays correct whatever the CGPM decides. On B012, which we both rank near the top, I note your WACQT and Chalmers ties and your own suggestion of recusal if it became the lead, and I treat that as a reason to keep it as an alternative and not as a leading candidate while the 2025 overlap is still unexplained.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, identifies novelty and timing as the main reservations and worries that Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work sits close to the 2005 recognition and so might reduce the standing of the clock itself.
responses.response: That is the sharpest form of the overlap question, and I would answer it in two parts. The comb is a tool that the lattice clock uses, as it uses an ultrastable laser, but the lattice-clock prize would be given for the atomic system and the interrogation scheme, not for the comb or the laser. Ye's contribution that is relevant to the citation is the accuracy and many-body operation of the lattice clock, not comb metrology, so I do not think his standing is diminished. On the chair's question about a second part, I looked again for a pairing and still find none that adds to the clock. B022 has the unresolved Blatt allocation, B012 follows the 2025 prize, B009 has the Krivanek gap, and B035 has the maturity issue. A two-part prize would dilute the clock without strengthening the configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the Katori and Ye pairing will be seen as adequate against the NIST, PTB, SYRTE and Tokyo contributions; I think it is, but it is a judgement, and I cannot verify the priority questions beyond the supplied evidence.
Exactly how narrowly the citation has to be worded to keep it separate from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I propose naming the optical lattice explicitly.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the SI redefinition; I treat it as neutral to the merits and would keep it out of the citation.
Whether circuit QED (B012) can be argued as distinct from the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize, which determines whether it remains a serious alternative.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I have no documented collaboration, supervisory or institutional tie to Katori or Ye. The chair's summary records my research stay in John Hall's laboratory and my work in laser spectroscopy and laser stabilisation as proximity to the B008 field, and I confirm it: Hall's 2005 prize is part of the precedent I am weighing, and I am a specialist in an adjacent technique. I judge this a field-proximity disclosure that the committee may want to discount, not grounds for recusal. For the alternatives, my Lund quantum-information and quantum-memory work is related to B022 and B012 only in subject area, and records no tie to the credited individuals. I would not oppose a discount of my vote on B008 if the committee wished to apply one.
